Accursed
uh-KUR-sid
adj. (devoted to destruction, under a ban or curse; rendering Hebrew cherem, Greek anathema)
From Old English acursod, cursed. It renders two heavy words — Hebrew cherem, a thing devoted irrevocably to God and therefore to destruction, and Greek anathema, which is that same word carried into the New Testament.

Biblical Definition

Accursed translates the Hebrew cherem, the ban: a thing so devoted to God that it may not be turned to any private use and must be destroyed. Jericho is placed under it, and the warning is exact: “keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse” (Joshua 6:18). Achan takes a garment, silver, and gold; the whole army is defeated at Ai; and the ban proves contagious, which is the point of the word. The Greek anathema carries it into the New Testament, where Paul uses it twice in ways that are almost unbearable to set side by side. He pronounces it on any preacher of another gospel, himself and angels included: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8). And he wishes it upon himself for his kinsmen's sake: “I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Romans 9:3). The same apostle who will not soften the curse on false teaching would take the curse himself if it could save Israel. Both are the same love, and the resolution of both is Galatians 3:13 — Christ was made a curse for us.

Webster 1828 Definition

Devoted to destruction under a ban. Jericho's cherem proves contagious through Achan; Paul pronounces anathema on any preacher of another gospel, and in the same epistles wishes himself accursed for his kinsmen.

expand to see more

ACCURSED, part. a. Doomed to destruction or misery. The city shall be accursed. Josh. 6.

2. Separated from the faithful; cast out of the church; excommunicated.

3. Worthy of the curse; detestable; execrable.

ANATHEMA, n. [Gr.] Excommunication with curses; a curse or denunciation by ecclesiastical authority.

4. In its original sense, a thing devoted or set apart, and hence irrevocably given up.

Key Scripture

Joshua 6:18 — "And ye, in any wise keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse, and trouble it."

Galatians 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Romans 9:3 — "For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:"

Galatians 3:13 — "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:"

Modern Corruption

Galatians 1:8 is used as a licence for anathematising every disagreement, while its actual scope — another gospel, a different way of being justified — is ignored; and in the opposite error the verse is dismissed as sub-Christian severity.

expand to see more

Paul's anathema is specific, and the specificity is the safeguard. He is not cursing men who differ on church polity, eschatology, or the mode of baptism; he is cursing the preaching of another gospel, which in Galatians means adding a work to faith as the ground of justification. The Judaizers of Galatia affirmed Christ, the resurrection, and the Scriptures; their error was one added requirement, and Paul treats it as the destruction of the gospel because a Christ who saves partly does not save at all. That precision is exactly what disappears when the verse is used to settle secondary controversies. A church that anathematises everything anathematises nothing in the end, because the word loses its edge through overuse — which is what happened to it in medieval and later ecclesiastical practice.

The opposite reaction, common now, treats Galatians 1:8 as an embarrassment: a lapse in temper, or first-century polemic we have outgrown. But Paul says it twice, deliberately, in consecutive verses, and includes himself and an angel from heaven in the scope — which is not the mark of a man losing control but of a man foreclosing every escape. The doctrinal reason is Romans 9:3 read alongside it: this same apostle would be damned in Israel's place if it were possible. He curses false gospels precisely because he loves the people they destroy. And the whole matter resolves at Galatians 3:13, where the curse falls on Christ instead of on us — which is why tampering with that gospel is the one thing Paul will not permit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew cherem (a thing devoted, banned, given over to destruction) from charam, to devote; Greek anathema (a thing set up or devoted, hence accursed), the Septuagint's rendering of cherem.

expand to see more

Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a devoted thing, a ban; the term governing Jericho in Joshua 6-7.

Hebrew charam (H2763) — to devote irrevocably, to destroy utterly; the verb behind the noun.

Greek anathema (G331) — a thing devoted to destruction, accursed; the word in Galatians 1:8-9, Romans 9:3, and 1 Corinthians 16:22.

Greek katara (G2671) — a curse; the word in Galatians 3:13, and epikataratos, cursed, in the quotation of Deuteronomy 21:23.

Greek anathema vs. anathema (G334, accented differently) — the same form also means a votive offering set up in a temple (Luke 21:5), preserving the original sense of a thing devoted.

Usage

"“Lest ye make yourselves accursed” — the ban is contagious, which is why Achan's theft defeated an army."

"“Though we, or an angel from heaven… let him be accursed” — Paul forecloses every exception including himself."

"“I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren” — the same man, the same love."
